sources: dossier=Net position: 'Replica-safety inside rimsky's core is advisory-lock-based: the dispatch tick takes a per-tick advisory lock (replicas failing to acquire skip the tick)' and Required behaviors: 'Per-tick advisory lock on dispatch; session advisory lock on migration batches; SQLite single-process posture (2026-05-04, foundation-contract, artifact)'; corroborated independently by concept:advisory-lock ('The scheduler-tick lock makes the tick safely multi-replica'); doc=replica.md:11 said scale=N is 'the union of N independent processes' and listed 'leader election' among coordination rimsky does NOT provide; code=scheduler.go tick() calls AdvisoryLocker.TrySchedulerTick, skips the sweep when another replica holds the lock, backed by pg_try_advisory_lock / sqlite flock with dedicated exclusion tests
note: The dossier and the sibling advisory-lock concept both establish that rimsky's runtime does provide one pinned per-tick coordination primitive (the scheduler tick), contradicting the doc's blanket 'union of N independent processes / no leader election' framing. Reworded the Definition to carve out the scheduler-tick exception while keeping the 'no generic replica coordination' thesis intact for every other role.

sources: dossier=same per-tick advisory lock passages as row 546; corroborated by concept:advisory-lock, which is a dedicated sibling concept documenting the scheduler-tick and claim-handle locks as the two pinned primitives on the same AdvisoryLocker interface; doc=replica.md Invariants (line 29, pre-edit) named only the supervisor's claim-handle lock as canonical and Boundaries (line 23, pre-edit) adjacency listed concept:supervisor/executor/publisher/sensor but never concept:advisory-lock or the scheduler-tick mechanism
note: The doc omitted a load-bearing sibling concept (concept:advisory-lock) that already documents the scheduler-tick lock as rimsky-provided replica coordination; a reader following replica.md's adjacency list had no path to it. There is no concept:scheduler artifact to cite (none exists in the catalog), so the fix points at concept:advisory-lock instead, which is the correct home per its own Boundaries section. Updated both the Boundaries adjacency list and the Invariants bullet to name the scheduler's per-tick lock alongside the supervisor's claim-handle lock.

sources: dossier=Net position: 'Rimsky models named peers (one per config entry), never pod counts. Replicas are not individually addressable... rimsky does not detect, heartbeat, or fail over replicas' (2026-05-17, sensor-messaging-unification); doc=replica.md Boundaries (line 23, pre-edit) said 'rimsky load-balances dispatch among reachable replicas' for executors; code=Resolver.Resolve returns a single Endpoint per executor name (StaticResolver is a single-value map lookup), peer/dial.go dials that one target with grpc's default pick_first policy, nothing enumerates or round-robins multiple replica endpoints
note: The dossier's 'named peers, never pod counts' thesis is exactly the general principle this specific claim violates: rimsky addresses one endpoint per name, not a pool it balances across. Code confirms single-endpoint resolution. Reworded the executor adjacency clause to attribute distribution across executor replicas to the deployment-tier load balancer/DNS behind the single resolved endpoint, not to rimsky itself.

sources: dossier=Net position: 'Replica-safety inside rimsky's core is advisory-lock-based' (i.e. the mechanism lives inside rimsky's own core, not merely 'the binary's implementation' as a thing separate from rimsky); Intentional absences: 'Advisory-lock-per-subscription / publisher HA machinery in rimsky - rejected; HA is the publisher implementation's responsibility' establishes the real boundary is rimsky's-own-role-binaries vs externally-authored binaries, not 'rimsky's runtime' vs 'the binary'; doc=replica.md Invariants (line 29, pre-edit) said multi-replica safety 'lives in the binary's implementation, not rimsky's runtime', immediately followed by its own canonical example (the supervisor's claim-handle lock), which is itself part of rimsky's runtime/foundation code
note: The phrase 'not rimsky's runtime' was imprecise rather than flatly false (a defensible reading survives), but it invites exactly the misreading the finding describes, and the dossier gives the correct boundary: rimsky's own role binaries (scheduler, supervisor) use rimsky-provided advisory-lock primitives; externally-authored binaries must coordinate on their own. Reworded the invariant to state that boundary directly instead of the runtime-vs-binary contrast.
